title: Polymorphism and Allotropy
description: When the same chemistry produces different solids

concepts.title: Same Atoms, Different Structures
concepts.contentHtml:
Polymorphism is the ability of a single chemical compound to exist in more than one crystal structure. When applied to a single element, it is also called allotropy.

The textbook example is carbon:

  • Diamond — tetrahedral sp³ network. Hardest natural material; transparent; electrically insulating; thermal-conductivity champion (5× copper).
  • Graphite — sheets of sp² hexagons; weak van der Waals between sheets. Soft and slippery; opaque; conducts electricity along the sheets.
  • Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) — sixty-atom soccer-ball molecules. Discovered 1985.
  • Carbon nanotubes — rolled-up graphene sheets, extreme strength and stiffness.
  • Graphene — a single 2-D atomic layer. Nobel Prize 2010.

One element, five radically different solids. Polymorphism is the rule rather than the exception in materials.

concepts.title: Iron's Allotropes
concepts.contentHtml:
Pure iron has four solid phases under different temperatures and pressures:

  • α-Fe (ferrite) — BCC, stable below 912 °C, ferromagnetic up to 770 °C (the Curie temperature).
  • γ-Fe (austenite) — FCC, stable 912–1394 °C, non-magnetic. Higher carbon solubility than α.
  • δ-Fe — BCC again, stable 1394–1538 °C; melts at 1538 °C.
  • ε-Fe — HCP, stable only at very high pressure (> ~13 GPa); thought to be the structure of Earth's inner core.

The α↔γ transition at 912 °C is the heart of every steel heat-treatment recipe. The same atoms, simply rearranging from BCC to FCC, change the carbon solubility from 0.02 % to 2.1 % — enabling the entire chemistry of austenitisation, quenching, and tempering.

concepts.title: Tin Pest and Other Cautionary Tales
concepts.contentHtml:
Polymorphism can ruin objects. Tin has two solid forms:

  • β-Sn (white tin) — BCT, stable above 13.2 °C. Familiar metallic shiny tin.
  • α-Sn (grey tin) — diamond cubic, stable below 13.2 °C. Brittle, dull-grey, semiconducting.

In sustained cold weather, the β → α transition turns metallic tin into crumbling grey powder — historically known as tin pest. Folklore blames the loss of Napoleon's pewter buttons in the 1812 Russian campaign on it (the historical evidence is weaker, but the chemistry is real).

Modern echoes: lead-free electronics solder is mostly tin, raising the risk of tin-pest in cryogenic spacecraft electronics. Engineers add small amounts of bismuth or antimony to suppress the transition. Polymorphism is a constant materials-engineering concern wherever extreme conditions are involved.

title: Classifying Phase Transitions
description: First-order, second-order, and the Ehrenfest scheme

concepts.title: First-Order Transitions
concepts.contentHtml:
Ehrenfest's scheme classifies transitions by which derivative of the free energy is discontinuous.

A first-order transition has a discontinuous first derivative of the Gibbs free energy — meaning a discontinuous jump in entropy and volume. Consequences:

  • A latent heat is absorbed or released.
  • The two phases coexist at the transition temperature (e.g. ice + water at 0 °C, 1 atm).
  • The transition involves a kinetic barrier: nucleation and growth of one phase inside the other.

Examples: melting, boiling, the α-γ transition in iron, the diamond-graphite transition (in principle, though kinetically frozen at room temperature).

concepts.title: Second-Order and Continuous Transitions
concepts.contentHtml:
A second-order transition has continuous first derivatives but discontinuous second derivatives — heat capacity, compressibility, and thermal expansion show jumps or divergences. There is no latent heat and no two-phase coexistence.

Classical examples:

  • Ferromagnetic Curie point — magnetisation goes continuously to zero. Iron at 770 °C, nickel at 358 °C.
  • Superconducting transition in zero magnetic field.
  • Order-disorder transitions in alloys — e.g. β-brass at 460 °C.
  • The λ-transition in liquid helium at 2.17 K, where He-II becomes a superfluid.

Modern theory replaced Ehrenfest's two-class scheme with a more general continuum: anything without a latent heat falls under continuous transitions, characterised by an order parameter that grows from zero at the transition with characteristic critical exponents.

concepts.title: Order Parameters and Symmetry Breaking
concepts.contentHtml:
A continuous transition is signalled by an order parameter that is zero in the symmetric (high-temperature) phase and grows continuously in the broken-symmetry (low-temperature) phase. Examples:

  • Magnetisation M for ferromagnets.
  • Density difference for liquid-gas at the critical point.
  • Long-range periodic ordering in displacive transitions.
  • Superconducting gap in the superconducting transition.

Near the transition, fluctuations of the order parameter span every length scale. This universality means that wildly different physical systems (a magnet and a fluid at its critical point) share the same critical exponents — one of the deepest results of 20th-century statistical mechanics, organised by the renormalisation group (Wilson, 1971).

title: Displacive vs Reconstructive Transitions
description: Two ways a crystal can rearrange itself

concepts.title: Displacive Transitions
concepts.contentHtml:
A displacive transition involves only small movements of atoms — typically a fraction of a bond length — without breaking nearest-neighbour bonds. The lattice subtly distorts; topology is preserved.

Classical example: the α-quartz to β-quartz inversion at 573 °C. The Si-O tetrahedra simply tilt and untilt; no Si-O bond breaks. The transformation is fast (essentially instantaneous, limited only by sound speed) and reversible. Quartz crystals heated past 573 °C and cooled back below it return to α-quartz with no degradation in crystal quality.

Displacive transitions often have small or no latent heat and are typically continuous or weakly first order. They are the basis of many ferroelectric, ferroelastic, and martensitic transitions.

concepts.title: Reconstructive Transitions
concepts.contentHtml:
A reconstructive transition rearranges atoms substantially: nearest-neighbour bonds break and reform, and the new structure has a topologically different connectivity. The transformation is slow, requires an activation barrier, and may not occur at all if the kinetics are too slow at the transition temperature.

Examples:

  • Quartz → tridymite → cristobalite in pure SiO₂ — each step requires breaking and reconnecting Si-O bonds and proceeds only slowly above 870 °C and 1470 °C respectively.
  • Diamond → graphite — thermodynamically favoured at room temperature and 1 atm, but kinetically frozen because the activation energy is enormous. Diamonds in your jewellery are technically metastable.

Many minerals routinely fail to convert at their nominal transition temperatures simply because the reconstructive step is too slow on geological timescales.

concepts.title: Why Polymorphs Often Get Stuck
concepts.contentHtml:
Many phases observable at room conditions are metastable — favoured by kinetics rather than thermodynamics:

  • Diamond at 1 atm, 25 °C — graphite is stable but the conversion barrier is too high.
  • White phosphorus at 25 °C — red phosphorus is stable, but conversion is slow without a catalyst.
  • Glass at 25 °C — crystal is the thermodynamic ground state, but the glass transition freezes the structure into an amorphous state.
  • Austenite at room temperature in stainless steel — stabilised against martensitic reversion by alloying with nickel.

Materials engineering routinely exploits metastability: nearly every modern engineering alloy depends on locking the system into a non-equilibrium state that can survive long enough to be useful, then resisting the slow drift toward true equilibrium.

title: Martensitic and Shape-Memory Transitions
description: Diffusionless transformations that build hard steel and bend wires back into shape

concepts.title: What Makes a Transition Martensitic
concepts.contentHtml:
A martensitic transition is a diffusionless, displacive, cooperative shear of the parent lattice into a new, lower-temperature daughter phase. Defining features:

  • Atoms move less than a single bond length, in coordinated fashion.
  • No diffusion required — the transformation can proceed at speeds approaching the speed of sound.
  • A specific orientation relationship exists between parent and product, often visible as a herringbone or plate microstructure.

The textbook case is steel: face-centred cubic austenite (γ) shears into body-centred tetragonal martensite (α') when quenched fast enough that carbon cannot diffuse. The trapped carbon is what makes martensite hard and brittle.

concepts.title: Nitinol and the Shape-Memory Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
Some martensitic transformations are reversible — heat the daughter phase up and it shears back into the parent. The most famous example is nitinol (NiTi, ~50:50 nickel and titanium):

  1. Above the austenite-finish temperature A_f, the alloy sits in a high-symmetry austenite phase.
  2. Cool below the martensite-finish temperature M_f and it shears into a low-symmetry martensite. The macroscopic shape changes only slightly because martensite forms in many crystallographic variants whose distortions cancel out on average.
  3. Bend the cold martensite — its variants reorient to accommodate the deformation, locking in a new shape.
  4. Heat above A_f — every variant reverses to the unique parent austenite. The wire snaps back to its original shape.

This is the shape-memory effect. Nitinol is used in self-expanding stents, eyeglass frames that survive bending, orthodontic archwires, and aerospace actuators.

concepts.title: Superelasticity
concepts.contentHtml:
If nitinol is held above A_f and stress is applied, the austenite locally transforms into stress-induced martensite — accommodating large strains (up to ~8 %) reversibly. When the stress is removed, austenite re-forms and the strain disappears.

This is superelasticity (or pseudoelasticity). Unlike conventional elastic strain in metals (limited to ~0.2 %), superelastic strain comes from a phase transformation, not bond stretching. It looks like rubber-like behaviour in a metal.

Practical consequences:

  • Nitinol stents can be compressed into a delivery catheter and released into an artery, where they self-expand and resist closure under arterial pulsation.
  • Nitinol eyeglass frames recover their shape after extreme bending.
  • Orthodontic wires apply a remarkably constant force across a large range of tooth movement.

All of this comes from a single underlying physics: a martensitic phase transition that is mechanically as well as thermally reversible.

title: The Glass Transition
description: When liquids forget how to crystallise

concepts.title: Glasses Are Frozen Liquids
concepts.contentHtml:
A glass is a non-crystalline (amorphous) solid produced by cooling a liquid fast enough that it cannot crystallise. The atoms remain in a liquid-like disordered configuration but lose mobility — they are 'frozen in' to their last fluid arrangement.

Common glass-formers:

  • Silicate glasses — ordinary window and bottle glass (mostly SiO₂ + Na₂O + CaO).
  • Polymers — polystyrene, PMMA, polycarbonate. Most thermoplastics are glassy at room temperature.
  • Metallic glasses — early alloys needed quenching at ~10⁶ K/s, but bulk glass-formers like Zr-Cu-Ni-Ti-Be need only ~1 K/s. Surprisingly elastic and corrosion-resistant.
  • Chalcogenide glasses — used in rewritable optical media (CD-RW) and emerging memory.

concepts.title: The Glass Transition Temperature T_g
concepts.contentHtml:
The glass transition temperature T_g is the temperature at which a cooled liquid loses macroscopic flow on experimental timescales. Below T_g it behaves as a solid (rigid, brittle, with crystal-like specific heat). Above T_g it behaves as a viscoelastic liquid.

T_g is a kinetic, not thermodynamic, transition: it depends on the cooling rate. Slower cooling gives lower T_g; faster cooling gives higher T_g. There is no true latent heat, but there is a step in heat capacity at T_g — a hallmark for differential scanning calorimetry.

Examples of T_g:

  • Window glass — about 550 °C.
  • Polycarbonate — about 145 °C.
  • PVC — about 80 °C.
  • Natural rubber — about −70 °C (which is why a rubber ball stays flexible in a household freezer but shatters like glass after a dip in liquid nitrogen).

Polymer T_g values determine which materials can be used as rigid plastics, which as flexible films, which as elastomers — and at what service temperatures.

concepts.title: Why Some Liquids Glass and Others Crystallise
concepts.contentHtml:
Whether a substance can be quenched into a glass depends on the competition between two timescales as it is cooled:

  • Crystallisation time — how quickly nuclei of the crystalline phase form and grow.
  • Vitrification time — how quickly viscosity rises, freezing the liquid.

Substances with strong, directional bonding (silica, polymers with bulky side groups, complex alloys) glass easily because crystallisation requires a great deal of atomic rearrangement that is slow even in the warm liquid. Substances that crystallise quickly (most pure metals) need extreme quench rates to glass at all — which is why bulk metallic glasses were a major engineering breakthrough.

Glasses age slowly. Stained-glass windows in medieval cathedrals are not measurably thicker at the bottom (a popular myth); the molecular relaxation timescales below T_g are vastly longer than 800 years. Glass is one of the slowest-evolving solids known.
